analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from cutting striking or locked-out workers' health coverage during labor disputes.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 56 Democratic sponsors, has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee since May 2025 with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers go on strike, or when an employer locks them out to pressure them in contract talks, employers can currently cut off the company health plan — which for many families is their only coverage. This bill would make that an illegal unfair labor practice, and add civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation ($150,000 for repeat offenders), including potential personal liability for company directors and officers who order it. It has been referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and has received no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: Unionized workers and their families who rely on employer-sponsored health insurance and would lose it during a strike or lockout under current rules. Keeping coverage during a dispute removes one of the employer's strongest pressure points, since a family can face losing insurance exactly when income has stopped.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from terminating or altering group health plan coverage for employees during a lawful strike [S2].
Prohibits employers from terminating or altering coverage for employees during a lockout aimed at pressuring them in collective bargaining [S2].
Creates civil penalties of up to $75,000 per violation for cutting coverage during a lockout, doubled to $150,000 for repeat violations or cases involving serious economic harm to an employee [S2].
Creates civil penalties of up to $50,000 per violation for cutting coverage during a lawful strike, doubled to $100,000 for repeat violations or cases involving serious economic harm [S2].
Allows the labor board to assess penalties personally against directors or officers who directed, committed, or had the authority to prevent such a violation [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use health coverage as leverage in labor disputes, including the cost of maintaining coverage through strikes and lockouts, and exposure to new civil penalties. Insurers and plan administrators would keep coverage active for more members during disputes, a modestly larger but less profitable-at-the-margin book.

drawbacks.text: Maintaining health coverage during strikes and lockouts is a real cost for employers, who would lose one of the few forms of economic pressure available when workers can be replaced only slowly or not at all [S2].

New penalties of up to $150,000 per violation, plus personal liability for officers and directors, could lead companies to restructure benefits, self-insure differently, or settle disputes differently to avoid the exposure [S2].

The bill protects coverage during a lawful strike but does not extend coverage to workers locked out for other reasons or to workers at non-union employers, leaving most of the private workforce untouched [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the benefit is large and direct: a family does not lose health insurance precisely when a strike has stopped their paycheck, which today can force a quick surrender in a contract fight. The cost falls on a narrower set of employers in active labor disputes, and it is genuinely a cost — coverage months are expensive. The main limits are scope (only strikes and lockouts, largely union situations) and enforceability, since the underlying labor enforcement process is slow even with new penalties on paper.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in May 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has had no hearing, markup, or floor action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Deluzio, joined by Rep. Sarah McBride, introduced the bill on May 21, 2025 [S1] [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce on the day of introduction and no further action appears in its history [S4].
It has 55 cosponsors, all Democrats, in addition to the sponsor [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers retain the ability to cut off health coverage during strikes and lockouts, which remains one of the strongest levers available to them in a contract dispute. Striking workers' families remain exposed to losing insurance mid-dispute.

sides.party_line_note: All 56 supporters — the sponsor and 55 cosponsors — are Democrats, with no Republican cosponsorship listed, and the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.note: Employers currently can cut group health coverage during a strike or lockout, which pressures workers to settle quickly; the bill removes that lever and adds civil penalties up to $150,000 with potential personal liability for officers.
More members would stay enrolled through strikes and lockouts rather than dropping off the plan, keeping premium revenue flowing; the effect is modest since these are existing covered workers.

Health coverage is a standard bargaining chip employers can pull mid-dispute; protecting it strengthens unions' ability to hold out for better contracts, which also protects non-union wage and benefit norms indirectly.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic support, no committee hearing or markup after months, and a committee majority that has not acted, the bill's realistic path is expiring quietly at the end of the 119th Congress unless labor policy moves up the agenda or a union campaign forces a hearing.
